title: Betrayed on his wedding day
text: In February 1815 the young sailor Edmond Dantès brings the ship Pharaon into Marseilles with everything ahead of him. The owner, M. Morrel, means to make him captain, his old father is waiting for him, and he is about to marry Mercédès, a girl from the Catalan village. But three men resent his luck: Danglars, the ship’s jealous supercargo; Fernand, Mercédès’s cousin, whom she has turned down; and Caderousse, an envious neighbour. Over drinks, Danglars writes an anonymous letter denouncing Dantès as a Bonapartist agent, pretends to throw it away as a joke, and Fernand quietly picks it up.

Dantès is arrested at his own wedding feast. The deputy prosecutor, Villefort, soon sees that he is innocent and is ready to free him, until he discovers that the letter Dantès carried from Elba is addressed to Villefort’s own father, the Bonapartist Noirtier. To protect his career, Villefort burns the letter and has Dantès shut away in the Château d’If, a grim island fortress, then rushes to Paris to warn King Louis XVIII of Napoleon’s plans and take the credit.

Napoleon does return, but only for a Hundred Days. During that time Villefort tricks Morrel into writing a petition for Dantès that makes him look like a dangerous Bonapartist, and keeps it. As chapter 13 closes, Waterloo has come and gone, Dantès lies forgotten in his dungeon, his enemies have moved on with their lives, and his father has died.

title: Fourteen years in darkness
text: In 1815 the young sailor Edmond Dantès was about to become a captain and marry Mercédès when three jealous men ruined him: Danglars, his shipmate; Fernand, Mercédès’s rejected cousin; and their drinking companion Caderousse. An anonymous letter denounced him as a Bonapartist, and the ambitious deputy prosecutor Villefort, who saw he was innocent but found that the letter he carried was addressed to Villefort’s own Bonapartist father, Noirtier, buried him in the island prison of the Château d’If.

Years pass. A prison inspector’s visit brings brief hope, but a note in Dantès’s file dooms him, and he decides to starve himself to death. Then he hears digging behind his wall. The tunneller is the Abbé Faria, a brilliant Italian scholar whom the jailers think mad. Faria works out for Dantès exactly who betrayed him, and why, and Dantès swears revenge. The old man teaches him languages, science and history, and they dig an escape tunnel together, until a fit leaves Faria paralysed.

Faria then shares his great secret: a vast treasure hidden by Cardinal Spada on the island of Monte Cristo. He names Dantès his heir and calls him his son. When a third attack kills the abbé, Dantès sews himself into his friend’s burial sack, but instead of being buried he is weighted with a cannonball and thrown off the cliffs into the sea.

As chapter 21 closes, Dantès has cut himself free, survived a storm, and been picked up by Genoese smugglers, who believe he is a shipwrecked Maltese sailor. It is 28 February 1829, fourteen years to the day since his arrest, and he renews his vow of revenge.

title: Treasure and a debt repaid
text: In 1815 the sailor Edmond Dantès was falsely denounced as a Bonapartist on his wedding day by Danglars and Fernand, with Caderousse looking on, and buried in the Château d’If by the prosecutor Villefort to protect his own father, Noirtier. In prison Dantès was educated by the Abbé Faria, who left him the secret of Cardinal Spada’s treasure. After fourteen years he escaped by taking the dead abbé’s place in a burial sack.

Sailing with smugglers, Dantès reaches the island of Monte Cristo, finds the treasure, and becomes immensely rich. Travelling as Lord Wilmore, he learns that his father is dead and Mercédès has vanished. Disguised as an Italian priest, he visits Caderousse, now a poor innkeeper, and hears the whole story: old Dantès starved to death; Danglars wrote the denunciation and Fernand posted it; Danglars is now a rich baron, and Fernand is the Count de Morcerf, married to Mercédès. The priest gives Caderousse a diamond.

Posing next as an English clerk of the Roman bank Thomson & French, Dantès buys up the debts of his old employer, M. Morrel, who has stood by him and is now close to ruin, and quietly takes the original denunciation from the prison records. He grants Morrel three months’ grace and tells his daughter, Julie, to obey a letter signed “Sinbad the Sailor.”

As chapter 30 closes, Morrel has been saved at the very moment he meant to shoot himself: Julie brought him a red purse holding his paid debt and a diamond for her dowry, and a new Pharaon sailed into port. His debts of gratitude repaid, Dantès now turns to vengeance.

title: Carnival in Rome
text: In 1815 Edmond Dantès was betrayed on his wedding day by the jealous Danglars and Fernand, with Caderousse looking on, and buried in prison by the prosecutor Villefort. After fourteen years he escaped, found the treasure of Monte Cristo that his fellow prisoner Faria left him, and learned that his enemies had prospered: Danglars is a baron, and Fernand is the Count de Morcerf, husband of Mercédès. Using the name “Sinbad the Sailor,” he secretly saved his old employer Morrel from ruin, then turned to vengeance.

Nine years later, in 1838, a young Parisian, Franz d’Épinay, lands on Monte Cristo and is entertained in a hidden underground palace by a mysterious host who calls himself Sinbad the Sailor. In Rome, Franz joins his friend Albert de Morcerf for the Carnival. Their innkeeper tells them about the bandit chief Luigi Vampa, who once met a traveller called Sinbad.

Franz soon recognises Sinbad’s voice in a cloaked man promising to save a condemned bandit, Peppino, and sees the same man at the opera with a beautiful Greek girl. He turns out to be their neighbour, the Count of Monte Cristo. The count charms Albert, takes the friends to an execution where Peppino is pardoned, and talks chillingly about revenge.

On the last night of Carnival, Vampa’s band kidnaps Albert. As chapter 37 closes, the count has walked into the bandits’ lair and won Albert’s freedom at once, and Albert is full of gratitude. Franz, though, noticed the count shudder as he shook Albert’s hand.

title: A house with a past
text: Edmond Dantès, betrayed in 1815 by Danglars and Fernand and buried in prison by the prosecutor Villefort, escaped after fourteen years with the treasure of Monte Cristo. Now known as the Count of Monte Cristo, he met Albert de Morcerf in Rome, rescued him from the bandit Luigi Vampa, and asked to be introduced to Paris society. Albert’s father is Fernand, now the Count de Morcerf.

The count arrives at Albert’s Paris breakfast on 21 May at exactly the hour agreed, and dazzles Albert’s friends: Debray, a minister’s secretary; Beauchamp, a newspaper editor; Château-Renaud; and Captain Maximilian Morrel, son of the shipowner Dantès once served, whom the count greets with visible emotion. Albert introduces him to his parents. The countess is Mercédès, and after his visit she anxiously warns her son to be careful.

The count buys a country house at Auteuil, and his Corsican steward, Bertuccio, turns pale at the address. In its garden, Bertuccio confesses, he once took vengeance on Villefort, who had refused justice for his murdered brother: he stabbed Villefort as he buried a newborn baby, then dug up the child and saved it. His sister-in-law raised the boy, Benedetto, who grew up cruel, tortured her for money and vanished. Bertuccio also witnessed Caderousse sell the abbé’s diamond and murder the jeweller who bought it, and was saved from the blame only by the Abbé Busoni.

Bertuccio believes he killed Villefort, but the count murmurs that the prosecutor may not be dead. As chapter 45 closes, he takes possession of his Paris house, and at midnight welcomes the Greek girl from Rome, Haydée, to her secret apartments.

title: Unlimited credit
text: Edmond Dantès, betrayed in 1815 by Danglars and Fernand and buried in prison by Villefort, escaped with a vast treasure and has arrived in Paris as the Count of Monte Cristo. Through Albert de Morcerf he has met Albert’s mother, Mercédès, and father, Fernand, now the Count de Morcerf. His steward Bertuccio has told him how he once stabbed Villefort at the Auteuil house the count has bought, and rescued the baby Villefort was burying there.

Now the count moves among his enemies. He humbles Baron Danglars, opening an “unlimited” credit with him and buying his wife’s prized horses. When those horses bolt with Madame de Villefort and her little son aboard, the count’s servant Ali stops them, and Villefort, very much alive and now a powerful royal prosecutor, comes to thank him. Villefort’s father, Noirtier, is paralysed. The count also gives Madame de Villefort, who is fascinated by poisons, a dangerous elixir.

Visiting Maximilian Morrel, his sister Julie and her husband Emmanuel, the count is deeply moved to see them treasure the relics of their unknown benefactor, “Sinbad the Sailor.” Maximilian, meanwhile, is secretly in love with Valentine de Villefort, who is unhappily engaged to Franz d’Épinay. At the opera, the count’s companion Haydée nearly faints on seeing Morcerf, who once served Ali Pasha at Yanina: this man, she says, sold her father to the Turks.
As chapter 54 closes, Albert dreads his arranged marriage to Danglars’ daughter, Eugénie, and the count is planning a dinner at Auteuil to which he expects a Major Cavalcanti and his son, Andrea.

title: Ghosts at Auteuil
text: Edmond Dantès, betrayed in 1815 by Danglars and Fernand and imprisoned by Villefort, has come to Paris as the fabulously rich Count of Monte Cristo. All three men are now powerful: Danglars a banker and baron, Fernand the Count de Morcerf and husband of Mercédès, Villefort a royal prosecutor. The count’s steward, Bertuccio, once stabbed Villefort in the garden of the count’s Auteuil house and rescued a baby Villefort was burying there.

The count brings two strangers onto the scene: Major Cavalcanti and his supposedly long-lost son, Andrea. Both, it turns out, are paid impostors, coached and funded by the count. He also bribes a telegraph operator to send false news that costs Danglars a fortune.

In the Villefort household, Valentine and Maximilian Morrel meet in secret by the garden gate. Her paralysed grandfather, Noirtier, who can speak only with his eyes, makes a will leaving his fortune to the poor if she marries Franz d’Épinay.

At the count’s Auteuil dinner, Bertuccio is horrified to recognise the guests: Madame Danglars is the woman who gave birth in that house, Villefort is the man he thought he had killed, and “Andrea Cavalcanti” is Benedetto, the baby he saved. As chapter 63 closes, the count has shown his guests the old bedroom and told them his workmen dug up a newborn’s skeleton in the garden. Madame Danglars has fainted, and Villefort has secretly asked to meet her.

title: Bread and salt
text: Edmond Dantès, betrayed in 1815 by Danglars and Fernand and imprisoned by Villefort, now moves through Paris as the Count of Monte Cristo, closing in on all three. Danglars is a banker, Fernand is the Count de Morcerf, married to Mercédès, and Villefort is royal prosecutor. The count has launched a young impostor, “Andrea Cavalcanti,” whom his steward Bertuccio has recognised as Benedetto, the baby Villefort buried at Auteuil.

Caderousse, escaped from the prison at Toulon, also recognises Andrea as Benedetto and begins blackmailing him. Danglars, losing money, coldly tells his wife he knows about her lovers, Villefort among them. He now prefers rich Andrea to Albert as a husband for Eugénie, sneers that Morcerf was once the fisherman Fernand Mondego, and, at the count’s hint, writes to Yanina for information about Morcerf’s past. Villefort confesses to Madame Danglars that he buried their newborn believing it dead, but the box later vanished: the child may have lived.

Alarmed, Villefort has the count investigated, but the Abbé Busoni and Lord Wilmore, both the count in disguise, give him only contradictory stories. At the Morcerfs’ ball, Mercédès notices that the count will eat nothing under her husband’s roof. Alone with him, she presses fruit on him and asks about his past, and he speaks of a girl he once loved who married another.
As chapter 71 closes, news arrives that the Marquis de Saint-Méran, Valentine de Villefort’s grandfather, has suddenly died.

title: Poison in the house
text: Edmond Dantès, betrayed in 1815 by Danglars and Fernand and imprisoned by Villefort, is now the Count of Monte Cristo, quietly closing in on all three in Paris. Danglars, a banker, has written to Yanina about the past of Fernand, now the Count de Morcerf. The young impostor “Andrea Cavalcanti,” really Villefort’s abandoned son Benedetto, is courting Danglars’ daughter, Eugénie, and Danglars is losing interest in a match between her and Albert de Morcerf.

Death strikes the Villefort house. The Marquise de Saint-Méran dies soon after her husband, insisting that Valentine marry Franz d’Épinay at once. Hiding in the garden, Maximilian Morrel hears Dr. d’Avrigny tell Villefort that she was poisoned. Franz is about to sign the marriage contract when the paralysed Noirtier shows him that his father, General d’Épinay, died in a fair duel with Noirtier himself. Franz breaks off the engagement, Noirtier makes Valentine his heir, and he lets Maximilian know they may marry once she comes of age.

Meanwhile Haydée tells Albert how her father, Ali Pasha of Yanina, was betrayed and killed, and how she and her mother were sold as slaves. When Beauchamp’s newspaper reports that a French officer named Fernand betrayed Yanina, Albert challenges Beauchamp to a duel.

As chapter 80 closes, Noirtier’s old servant Barrois has died after drinking his master’s lemonade, which was poisoned. Dr. d’Avrigny accuses Valentine of the deaths; Villefort refuses to give up his daughter, the doctor withdraws, and the frightened servants all leave.

title: A challenge accepted
text: Edmond Dantès, betrayed in 1815 by Danglars and Fernand and imprisoned by Villefort, has become the Count of Monte Cristo. In Paris his enemies are falling. Death has struck Villefort’s house again and again, poison is to blame, and the doctor suspects Valentine. The impostor “Andrea Cavalcanti,” really Benedetto, is now engaged to Danglars’ daughter, Eugénie.

Caderousse, blackmailing Andrea, is sent by him to rob the count’s house. Forewarned, the count catches him and, as the Abbé Busoni, makes him write a letter exposing Andrea. Outside, an accomplice stabs Caderousse. Dying, he names Benedetto as his killer, and the count reveals his true identity to him before he dies.

Beauchamp finds proof in Yanina that Albert’s father betrayed Ali Pasha and generously lets Albert burn it, but the story breaks anyway while the count has Albert at his house in Normandy. Before the Chamber of Peers, Morcerf defends himself well until Haydée appears with proof that he betrayed her father and sold her and her mother into slavery. Morcerf is ruined. Learning from Danglars that it was the count who advised him to write to Yanina, Albert turns his fury on Monte Cristo.

Mercédès begs her son to stay friends with the count, but Albert insults him publicly at the Opera. As chapter 88 closes, the count has accepted the challenge, sworn that he will kill Albert, and asked Maximilian Morrel and Emmanuel to be his seconds.

title: A wedding undone
text: Edmond Dantès, betrayed in 1815 by Danglars and Fernand and imprisoned by Villefort, returned as the Count of Monte Cristo to take his revenge. Fernand, the Count de Morcerf, has been exposed as the traitor of Yanina, and his son, Albert, challenged the count to a duel.

The night before the duel, Mercédès comes to the count, calls him Edmond, and begs for her son’s life. He shows her the letter that sent him to prison, then promises that Albert will live, which means letting Albert kill him. But at dawn Albert apologises before everyone, saying the count had every right to his revenge. Albert and Mercédès give up the Morcerf name and fortune. When Morcerf comes to challenge him, the count reveals that he is Edmond Dantès. Morcerf flees home, watches his wife and son leave him, and shoots himself.

In the Villefort house, Valentine collapses after drinking from a glass of water. Maximilian confesses his love for her to the count, who is horrified that he loves a Villefort but promises she will not die. Noirtier has been protecting her by accustoming her to the poison, and the Abbé Busoni rents the house next door.

Danglars, close to ruin, needs Eugénie’s marriage to Andrea, and she reluctantly agrees. As chapter 96 closes, the grand contract signing has collapsed: the count told of a bloodstained waistcoat found with a letter to Danglars, and police arrived to arrest Andrea for Caderousse’s murder. But Andrea has vanished.

title: Mourning and a promise
text: Edmond Dantès, betrayed in 1815 by Danglars and Fernand and imprisoned by Villefort, came back as the Count of Monte Cristo. Fernand, exposed as a traitor, has shot himself, and Mercédès and Albert have left his house and name behind. The impostor “Andrea Cavalcanti,” really the escaped convict Benedetto, fled his wedding to Eugénie Danglars but has been caught at an inn at Compiègne. Eugénie herself has run away in disguise with her friend Louise d’Armilly, and Villefort has refused Madame Danglars’ plea to go easy on Andrea.

The count, watching from the house next door, has been swapping Valentine de Villefort’s poisoned drinks for safe ones. One night he steps into her room and tells her to pretend to sleep. She watches her stepmother, Madame de Villefort, pour poison into her glass, hoping Valentine’s fortune will pass to her own son, Edward. The count gives Valentine a pill and tells her to fear nothing, even if she wakes in a tomb.

By morning Valentine lies cold and still, and Dr. d’Avrigny pronounces her dead. Noirtier privately tells Villefort who the killer is, and Villefort vows to deal with it within three days. On the morning of her funeral, the count walks off with five million francs that Danglars owed to the hospitals, and the banker secretly prepares to flee France.

As chapter 105 closes, Valentine has been buried at Père-Lachaise. The count has followed the grief-stricken Maximilian home and stopped him from shooting himself by revealing that he is Edmond Dantès, the Morrel family’s secret benefactor, and Maximilian has promised to live for one more month.
